Chapter 41

Tests that find real bugs

Property-based, fault injection, load — and an honest account of which kinds actually caught something.

By the end of this chapter

Write tests that assert invariants rather than paths, and know which kind to reach for.

This project has a large test suite. It is worth being honest about which parts of it earned their keep, because the answer is not what a testing pyramid would predict.

Assert invariants, not paths

A path test says "given this input, expect this output". It catches the case you thought of. An invariant says "whatever happens, this must remain true" — and it catches the case you did not.

The venue has four, and almost every valuable test in this repository is one of them wearing a different hat:

  1. The books balance. Every posting sums to zero, so trialBalance() is always 0.
  2. No order is overfilled. filled <= quantity for every order, always.
  3. The book is never crossed. In continuous trading, the best bid is below the best ask.
  4. Replay is deterministic. Rebuilding from the log produces a state with the same fingerprint.

You can assert all four after literally anything — a fuzz run, a crash, ten thousand random orders — without knowing what was supposed to happen.

Property-based testing

fast-check generates hundreds of random sessions and checks the property after each. When it finds a failure it shrinks it — repeatedly simplifying the input while the failure persists — so what you get is not a 120-step session but the three orders that actually matter.

Shrinking is the feature. A random failure you cannot reduce is barely more useful than a bug report. The four-order counterexample that fits in a comment is what turns "the fuzzer found something" into a fix.

Fault injection

One of these found a genuinely dangerous bug. The test handed the engine a corrupt snapshot — a truncated JSON body — and asserted it still recovered. It did not: deserialise threw body.instruments is not iterable, the error escaped recover(), and the engine refused to start. A file that exists purely as an *optimisation* had become a single point of failure for the whole venue.

The fix, which chapter 15 walks through with its full comment, treats a snapshot that will not parse as absent: recovery replays from genesis instead, more slowly and correctly. It logs as it does so, because a venue that quietly replays from genesis on every start is one whose snapshots have been broken for months.

Load, and the bug that killed the engine

Ten thousand orders. The engine died partway through:

An error about opening a database, from code that had the database open the entire time. Measuring /proc/self/fd after a thousand transactions told the story:

@libsql/client 0.17.4's transaction() opened a second connection and never released it — not on commit, not on rollback, not on an explicit close(). Two descriptors per transaction, forever. The engine opens one transaction per command, so at the default file limit it died after about ten thousand orders. The first fix was BEGIN IMMEDIATE and COMMIT as plain statements on the one connection; 0.18 then fixed the leak with a connection pool, which made that impossible — a statement borrows a connection and the pool rolls back whatever it left open — and withTransaction went back to transaction(), this time with the leak gone:

The promise chain is what serialises callers, and the pool made it more necessary rather than less. On one connection, two overlapping withTransaction calls would put their statements into *one* transaction and commit them together — not a deadlock, not an error, and completely wrong. On a pool, each gets its own connection and the second BEGIN IMMEDIATE waits for the first's write lock inside a synchronous native call — blocking the event loop that the first transaction needs in order to finish. A deadlock with a five-second timeout on it. The chain makes the second caller wait in JavaScript, where waiting is free.

And the regression test still measures file descriptors directly. It is a test of the library now, and the library has been wrong about this once — so if a release leaks again it fails in two seconds instead of in production after a few minutes of real trading.

The tests that were wrong

Four of my own, because a course that only shows the tests that worked is teaching something false.

  • A helper used the default batchSize: 200, so the first callback reported everything already applied and the test proved nothing.
  • The same helper hung when the target sequence had already been passed before it started waiting.
  • A load test asserted 10,000 order_record rows and got 2,582 — 7,418 were correctly rejected by the fat-finger collar. The right assertion was accepted + rejected === COUNT.
  • expect(JSON.stringify(keys)).not.toContain(':') — meant to prove no secret leaked. JSON itself is full of colons. It passed nothing and failed nothing.

A vacuous test is worse than no test, because it occupies the space where a real one would go and reports green while doing it. Whenever you write an assertion, break the code deliberately and check the test actually fails.

What actually found the bugs

A browser at 390px found two layout bugs no unit test could see. curl found four API bugs in an afternoon. A load test found a file-descriptor leak. Fault injection found the corrupt-snapshot dependency. A property test found a crossed book. The single highest-value habit in this whole project was running the thing, repeatedly, in the shape a real user would.

Six browser tests, each of which failed first

A unit test cannot see what a person sees when the venue refuses them, so a short Playwright suite in apps/web/e2e/ does. Six tests, run against the production build by pnpm verify, each making the venue say no — or fail — for a real reason and asserting what the person is told:

  • A venue operator's positions panel. The refusal used to take the whole terminal down with it, and the first fix still served the working terminal as an HTTP 403. The test now checks the page after signing in *and* after a reload, status included (chapter 27).
  • An auditor's cancel. Refused at the gateway, and the screen used to show nothing at all (chapter 24).
  • A trader opening the risk console. Used to get SvelteKit's built-in error page, because the app had no +error.svelte of its own (chapter 27).
  • A wrong password. Used to replace the sign-in form with an error page (chapter 25).
  • A wrong password, with JavaScript switched off. Used to come back in the page, in plain text, in the password field and in the hydration data (chapter 25).
  • A positions read that fails. Used to leave the panel stuck until a full reload; now it can be tried again in place (chapter 27).

The warning above was applied to them literally. Every one was run against the code from before its fix — the old pages, the new tests — and every one failed, each for its own reason: no Tape heading (and, against the two half-fixes since, a refusal where the note belongs, or a 403 on reload); no alert; no failure card; no form; the password found in the page; no Try again button. A test that had passed there would have been testing nothing.

They are the only tests in the project that open a browser. Every other test is Vitest running in Node — no window, no clicks, just functions and real SQLite files — and that is faster, steadier and easier to read. This project once deleted Playwright altogether, for being a dependency with nothing to run. Bringing it back was a decision that had to be earned, so here is the case.

Why these six need a browser

Each bug was in how the server, the network and the page meet, and showed only on the page. Svelte's documentation draws the line for the clearest one — errors "occurring outside the rendering process (for example, in event handlers …) are not caught by error boundaries" — so a refused cancel is handled by the try in its own handler or by nothing, and only a click runs that handler. Two cheaper shapes were weighed. Svelte's testing guide says to ask first whether the logic can be lifted out and tested on its own — and the one piece that could be, was: reading the message from a refusal started as a hand-written reader pasted into three components, and is now messageFrom in #lib/errors.ts, built on isHttpError and tested by Vitest (chapter 24). Everything left is wiring — a promise nobody caught, an await in the wrong place, a refusal caught where it should have been a branch, a boundary that could never be reached, an error that should have been invalid, a field name that decides what a page echoes back. Mounting the terminal under jsdom with its remote functions mocked fails differently: a mock rejects with whatever its author believes a refusal looks like, and believing it was an Error was the bug. A test that mocks the thing it is about asserts the assumption. So the case was checked rather than argued: with the Cancel button put back to void cancelOrder(...), every Vitest test passes, and this suite fails because no alert ever appears.

Chromium is a one-off download. After that, verify runs the browser tests last, against the build it has just made:

The second line is the one that is easy to leave out. It waits for an attribute the root layout sets:

Wait for hydration, not for time

Server rendering puts every button on the screen before any of them has a handler. A test that clicks in that gap clicks nothing, then times out waiting for a reaction that was never coming — which looks exactly like the bug it was written to catch. An $effect only runs in a browser, once the component is mounted, so the attribute appears at precisely the moment the page can respond. Waiting for it costs nothing on a fast machine and is still correct on a slow one, which no waitForTimeout can say.

The test once ended with one more line: await expect(cancel).toBeVisible(), under the comment "Refused at the gateway, so the order never left the book". It could not fail. No engine runs under the browser suite, so no order's status ever changes, and the Cancel button stays on screen whether the cancel was accepted or refused. The alert is the assertion. The extra line was the vacuous kind the warning above is about, and it went.

The first draft of that test signed in as a trader and cleared the cookies, to stand in for an expired session. It failed for the wrong reason: the terminal was still settling after the sign-in redirect, something on it met the missing cookie before the click did, and the whole page went to the error page. Changing state underneath a page that is still loading tests the loading, not the thing you meant. The auditor is refused every time, and is the commoner case anyway.

The last piece is where the suite gets its venue. The seed deletes the file it is given, so the database is pinned in the config rather than read from the environment, and the server is never one that happened to be running already:

Why never reuse a running server

Reusing a server that is already up saves a few seconds locally, and reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI is a line plenty of Playwright configs carry — this one did, at first. Here it would quietly break both promises above: the seed is part of the server's command, so a reused server never seeds, and it serves whichever database it was started with. A failure that says "port 4173 is already in use" costs ten seconds to act on. A green run against the wrong venue costs whatever somebody does next on the strength of it.

Checkpoint

  • You can name the venue's four invariants and assert them after any operation
  • You can explain what shrinking gives you that a random failure does not
  • You can explain why a corrupt snapshot must not stop the engine
  • You can explain why a vacuous test is worse than a missing one
  • You can explain why each browser test was run against the old code, and why they wait for data-hydrated
  • You can say why these six tests need a browser when every other test here runs in Node, and why mocking the remote functions would not have caught the bug
  • You can explain why the positions test reloads the page and checks the status, and why the password test switches JavaScript off
